explanation: Lock definition (ch28 p310) answers 'what does a lock guarantee' and ch31 p363-364 give binary semaphore with initial value 1; both chapters genuinely needed and answer is correct.

Answer blends the two cases into one 'looping on a flag' thread, attributing the p323 lock-spinning time-slice waste to the join case and never explicitly answering 'both?'; it also omits that a condition variable puts the waiter to sleep.
suggested_fix: Add evidence (p346): "What we would like here instead is some way to put the parent to sleep until the condition we are waiting for (e.g., the child is done executing) comes true." | Replace expected_output with: "Yes, spinning is wasteful in both cases. When spinning on a lock whose holder has been switched out, the waiting thread can waste an entire time slice checking a value that isn't going to change. When a parent spins on a flag waiting for a child to finish, it works but is hugely inefficient because the parent wastes CPU time. The better option for waiting on another thread is a condition variable: an explicit queue the waiting thread puts itself on (going to sleep) until another thread changes the condition and signals it."

explanation: Answer says empty/full alone always race, but p367-368 show they work for a single-slot buffer; the race appears with MAX > 1 and multiple producers/consumers overwriting the same slot. It also omits that naively wrapping the waits in the mutex deadlocks (p368-369).
suggested_fix: Add evidence (p368): "Let us now imagine that MAX is greater than 1 (say MAX = 10)." | Add evidence (p368): "Producer Pb starts to run, and at line f1 it also puts its data into the 0th element of buffer, which means that the old data there is overwritten!" | Add evidence (p368): "The filling of a buffer and incrementing of the index into the buffer is a critical section, and thus must be guarded carefully." | Add evidence (p369): "As you can see, we simply move the mutex acquire and release to be just around the critical section; the full and empty wait and signal code is left outside." | Replace expected_output with: "With condition variables, always recheck the condition in a while loop, not an if, because of Mesa semantics. With semaphores, the empty and full semaphores alone are not enough once the buffer has more than one slot and there are multiple producers or consumers: filling a buffer entry and incrementing the index is a critical section, so without mutual exclusion two producers can write the same slot and data is overwritten. The fix is a mutex held only around put()/get(), with the empty/full waits left outside it; putting the mutex around the semaphore waits causes deadlock."

explanation: Answer says LRU relies on temporal locality, but p257 quote only defines temporal locality in a sidebar; nothing quoted ties recency-based replacement to it, nor links page caching and TLB under one principle.
suggested_fix: Add evidence (p256): "For example, if a program has accessed a page in the near past, it is likely to access it again in the near future." | Add evidence (p257): "The assumption of the presence of these types of locality plays a large role in the caching hierarchies of hardware systems, which deploy many levels of instruction, data, and address-translation caching to help programs run fast when such locality exists."

explanation: Question asks WHY LRU dies on a slightly-too-big loop, but the answer only restates that it does (and opens with 'Yes' to a why-question); it never explains that LRU evicts exactly the oldest page the loop needs next, nor corrects the premise that LRU is always smart.
suggested_fix: Add evidence (p259): "These algorithms, under a looping-sequential workload, kick out older pages; unfortunately, due to the looping nature of the workload, these older pages are going to be accessed sooner than the pages that the policies prefer to keep in cache." | Add evidence (p259): "Indeed, even with a cache of size 49, a looping-sequential workload of 50 pages results in a 0% hit rate." | Replace expected_output with: "LRU is only a good bet when the workload has locality, so it is not always the smart choice. In a loop slightly larger than the cache, LRU evicts the oldest page, which is exactly the one the loop will need again soonest. For a TLB of size n, a program looping over n + 1 pages makes LRU miss on every access, whereas random does much better. For page replacement, a looping-sequential workload is a worst case for both LRU and FIFO: even with a cache of 49 pages, looping over 50 pages gives a 0% hit rate, while Random at least gets some hits."

explanation: Linear-table size problem (ch18 p199) and multi-level tables (ch20 p230-231) are both needed; answer is correct and its 4MB example matches the quote.

For 'what happens', the answer stops at detection and eviction policy; it omits that the page-fault handler finds the disk address in the PTE, reads the page in, updates the PTE and retries (p244-245), and the 'must evict first' step is better supported by p245.
suggested_fix: Add evidence (p244): "When the OS receives a page fault for a page, it looks in the PTE to find the address, and issues the request to disk to fetch the page into memory." | Add evidence (p245): "Thus, the OS might like to first page out one or more pages to make room for the new page(s) the OS is about to bring in." | Add evidence (p245): "When the disk I/O completes, the OS will then update the page table to mark the page as present, update the PFN field of the page-table entry (PTE) to record the in-memory location of the newly-fetched page, and retry the instruction." | Replace expected_output with: "The page-table entry's present bit is zero, meaning the page is on disk, so the access is a page fault and the OS page-fault handler runs. It looks in the PTE for the page's disk address and issues a request to fetch the page. Because memory is full, the OS first has to page out one or more pages to make room, and which page to evict is decided by its replacement policy. When the disk I/O completes, the OS marks the page present, records the new PFN in the PTE, and retries the instruction."
